This was our Saturday class in Bangkok with @boonchutanti. The teacher counts, and the whole room moves on the same breath.
This class did the second and third Ashtanga series (Intermediate and Advanced A). The heat builds. Sweat runs into your eyes.
Alone, it is easy to stop here. In the room, the count keeps going, so you keep going.
You forget you are tired. You stop trying so hard. You just breathe and move.
Most long-time practitioners know this moment. That letting go is the advanced part.
Want to try a class with us in Bangkok? Comment TRIAL and we'll message you.

Filmed at our workshop in Guangzhou, China, with @boonchutanti and @missjamsai.
After a class of the second Ashtanga series and part of the third, students work on backbends, scorpion handstands and the tic-toc. From a handstand, drop into a backbend, and kick back up.
Most people think about throwing the body back. These students think about how each joint should move.
Shoulders, chest, back, hips and legs move together. One breath, one rhythm.
This ability is not natural. It is built slowly, with clear guidance, hands-on help and the right preparation for each joint.

This is longevity. Not in theory. On the mat, every morning.
Thank you for showing us what is possible.

caption:
This is Bakasana B (crane asana, also called crow). You jump from hands and feet straight onto your arms, knees on your upper arms.
Strong arms help, but they are not enough. The breath and a strong middle hold you there.
Follow the words on screen. Breathe in and jump. Hold the belly. Breathe out slowly as the knees touch the arms. Then stay for five breaths.
Bandha means a light lock low in the belly. You breathe with it and push back with it. Then you breathe out and land.
This was our Saturday led Intermediate class (the second Ashtanga series) at AYBKK with @boonchutanti. Led means the teacher calls every breath and the whole room moves together.
Want to try a class with us in Bangkok? Comment TRIAL and we'll message you.

This is Bhujapidasana, the arm-squeeze asana. You jump your legs around your arms, hook the feet, bend the elbows and bring the head down.
Then you stay for five breaths. Breathe in, breathe out, belly in. You can hear the teacher count.
The power comes from steady, even breathing. It also keeps your energy going.

Don't feel like practicing today? That's the day that counts.

Not just more work. Work you don't feel like doing.

On screen: one week of our classes. Mysore (you move at your own pace and the teacher helps you one by one) and led classes (everyone moves together to the teacher's count).

Same practice, same time, a teacher who notices. On the hard mornings, the room carries you.

truth_notes: The voice is not Boonchu's. It is a podcast clip, credited '@hubermanlab podcast' in the original caption. It's not about adding more work. It's about adding more work that you don't want to do. This brain area gets bigger... smaller in obese people, gets bigger when they diet, larger in athletes... grows larger in people that see themselves as challenged and overcome some challenge.' The footage is one week of classes: a full room, close-ups of students, backbends, headstands. caption:
Is 64 too old to get strong and flexible?
This uncle lives in China and comes to Bangkok to practice for a month or two at a time.
When he first came, his body was stiff and he muscled through every movement. But he never gave up.
Then one day I saw him come up from his backbend almost all the way on his own.
This is Friday Mysore with @boonchutanti and @missjamsai. In a Mysore class everyone does their own practice at their own pace, and the teacher helps each person one by one.
Ashtanga is for people who keep showing up and improve step by step, no matter how old they are.
